The folder `data/` holds the data behind a published data story, "What Makes an Album the Greatest of All Time?": https://pudding.cool/2024/03/greatest-music/
The files: data/albums.csv, data/voters.csv

Write down the story's findings that this data reproduces.

1. Read the story on the web. web_fetch returns the page as the server sends it. web_view opens it in a browser and scrolls it like a reader, so it also gets text drawn by scripts, chart labels and the text of scrolling steps: use it when web_fetch returns little of the story, and to read what the charts label. Follow links to the story's methods or data notes when they say how a number was computed.
2. List every finding the authors draw from data: each number, comparison, ranking, share, trend or pattern the text states or a chart labels. A description of the data itself is not a finding: how many records, people, items, categories or sources it has, and how it was collected. When a chart states the same thing for each of its items (the top three for each phrase, the share for each year), that is one finding, written as one fact whose code computes it for every item at once.
3. Write each finding the files in data/ can reproduce as a fact in `facts.json`:

```json
[{"id": "women-front-shorter",
  "source": "On average, the pockets in women's jeans are 48% shorter and 6.5% narrower than men's pockets.",
  "claim": "Women's front pockets average 14.3 cm of maximum height against 23.1 cm for men.",
  "tables": {"m": "data/measurements.csv"},
  "code": "m.groupby('menWomen').maxHeightFront.mean()"}]
```

- `id`: unique in the file, a few meaningful words.
- `source`: the story's own words for this finding, quoted exactly, from its text or a chart label.
- `claim`: the finding in one sentence, with the numbers the code prints, and nothing the printout does not show: the story's own wording and numbers belong in `source`, not in the claim.
- `tables`: the files the code reads, each a variable name and the file's path from this folder, such as `data/orders.csv`; every file is read with `pd.read_csv(path)`.
- `code`: one Python expression over those variables, with `pd` (pandas) and `np` (numpy) available: the plain pandas computation whose printout shows the finding, such as a filter, a group-by, a count, a share or a sort. Do not assemble the result into a hand-made Series or dict.

Evaluate every fact from this folder the way it will be checked: read its `tables` with `pd.read_csv`, evaluate its `code`, print the value the way pandas prints it, and read the printout against the claim and the source. Every number, name and comparison in the claim must be in the printout, computed from the tables: code that writes a number itself, such as a string or a Series of typed-in values, does not count. The printout must agree with the story's numbers, up to rounding. Use the story's own definitions and filters, from its text or methods: a term means the same in every fact (if making it past the rookie contract is more than two seasons in one fact, it is more than two seasons in all of them), and a range, threshold or subset is one the story uses, never one chosen to make a number come out right. If the story's number only comes out under a definition or filter the story does not use, the finding is not reproduced. If after a fair try the data does not give the story's number (it needs other data, a different period, or the numbers differ beyond rounding), leave the finding out of facts.json.

4. Write `skipped.json`: every finding you left out, as [{"source": "the story's words", "why": "..."}].

Deliver both files, even when the data reproduces none of the story's findings: then `facts.json` is `[]`.
I'll start by exploring the data files and reading the story.

This certitude wasn’t to last, though.
2020

Beyond “What’s Going On” jumping from #6 to #1 and “Pet Sounds” remaining locked in at #2, the entire top 10 was changed, some albums jumping scores of spots.

The “new” greatest albums of all time
Many of these albums were released over the past decade, such as Kanye West’s “My Beautiful Dark Twisted Fantasy” (#17).
And Kendrick Lamar’s “To Pimp a Butterfly” (#19).
And Beyoncé’s “Lemonade” (#32).
And Frank Ocean’s “Blonde” (#79).
But other additions had been out for a long time, like Kate Bush’s “Hounds of Love,” originally released in 1985.
And Joy Division’s “Unknown Pleasures” (1979).
Some new additions came from even further in the past. Billie Holiday’s “Lady in Satin” made the list in 2020 despite being unranked in 2003, 45 years after its release.
In short, beyond accounting for new releases, there must be other factors influencing
’s choices.
This project uses
album rankings – twenty years apart in time – to determine what influences “greatness”.
First, musical greatness is shaped by how we listen.
Medium
Just a moment ago, we noted the turnover in
’s 2020 ranking: a third of the albums from 2003 did not make the 2020 list.
Rolling Stone’s
Ranking of Greatest Albums

the 2003 ranking
that failed to rank twenty years later.

, Unranked in
18% are compilations or greatest hits albums. These types of albums were popular in the days of physical releases, like CDs, cassettes, and vinyl. Today, official greatest hits collections have largely been
. In short, these types of albums have lost some of their prestige.
replaced by ever-evolving playlists
6% of the albums are also not currently available on Spotify.
For example, Captain Beefheart’s “Trout Mask Replica” was #58 in 2003. 17 years later, it failed to rank.
It’s hard for an album to remain relevant if most people don’t have a means to listen to it.

In short, after a certain point, when people are talking about great albums of the 1950s, they are likely talking about Miles Davis’s “Kind of Blue,” Elvis Presley’s self-titled album, and Frank Sinatra’s “In the Wee Small Hours,” among a few others.
Is it possible in 100 years that some obscure album from the 1950s will suddenly be hailed as the decade’s masterpiece? Yes. But it’s not likely. Some level of consensus does seem to appear over time, despite all of the unexpected non-musical factors that influence list construction.

This project began with a Google sheet created by
Chris Eckert
Rolling Stone's 500 Greatest Albums 2003 v 2012 v. 2020
This dataset is actually misleading, because the 2003 ranking seems to come from a book published by
, where the editor chose to change the original ranking: "For the book version of the RS 500 I have eliminated a few compilation albums that simply repeated material appearing elsewhere on albums that made the list. I've also combined the two volumes of Robert Johnson's ‘King of the Delta Blues Singers’ into the more readily available ‘Complete Recordings.’ That left room for eight new albums to bubble up from the bottom of our tally."
For this project, we decided to use
original ranking, which you can find on the Internet Archive
here
. (We also acquired the original print magazine issue, published in 2003). The 2003 judges come from the magazine and book. 2020 judges are available
).

content.text:
Title: What Makes an Album the Greatest of All Time?
URL Source: https://pudding.cool/2024/03/greatest-music/
Published Time: Mon, 06 Jul 2026 15:03:17 GMT
Markdown Content:
[![Image 1: The Pudding logo mark](https://pudding.cool/2024/03/greatest-music/assets/logo.png)](https://pudding.cool/)
![Image 2: series of cover art from the rolling stone 500 greatest albums of all time](https://pudding.cool/2024/03/greatest-music/assets/img3.png)
The Remaining Top 10
#251 - 500
#1 Greatest Album
2003 Ranking
![Image 3: Ranked #1 in 2003, Cover art for The Beatles's Sgt. Pepper's Lonely Hearts Club Band](https://pudding.cool/2024/03/greatest-music/assets/album_art_resized/full/6QaVfG1pHYl1z15ZxkvVDW.jpg)
#11 - #250
In 2003, _Rolling Stone_ magazine released its “500 Greatest Albums of All Time,” placing the Beatles’ “Sgt. Pepper’s Lonely Hearts Club Band” in the top slot.
![Image 4: Sgt. Pepper's Lonely Hearts Club Band](https://pudding.cool/2024/03/greatest-music/assets/album_art_resized/256/6QaVfG1pHYl1z15ZxkvVDW.jpg)
When the publication updated the list in 2012 to include the first decade of the new millennium, not only did the Beatles’ classic remain at #1 but the entire top 10 was unchanged.
This certitude wasn’t to last, though.
_Rolling Stone_ revised the list in 2020 again, and the two decade consensus was no more.
Beyond “What’s Going On” jumping from #6 to #1 and “Pet Sounds” remaining locked in at #2, the entire top 10 was changed, some albums jumping scores of spots.
Once again, here’s the 2003 ranking from twenty years ago. We’ve highlighted those albums that made the top 10 in 2020.
But each year’s ranking isn’t just the same albums shuffled throughout the 500 slots.
Here is the complete ranking from 2020, and nearly a **third** of the albums were new, never appearing in previous rankings. Let's examine a few of these albums.
The “new” greatest albums of all time
Many of these albums were released over the past decade, such as Kanye West’s “My Beautiful Dark Twisted Fantasy” (#17).
![Image 5: My Beautiful Dark Twisted Fantasy](https://pudding.cool/2024/03/greatest-music/assets/album_art_resized/256/20r762YmB5HeofjMCiPMLv.jpg)
And Kendrick Lamar’s “To Pimp a Butterfly” (#19).
![Image 6: To Pimp a Butterfly](https://pudding.cool/2024/03/greatest-music/assets/album_art_resized/256/7ycBtnsMtyVbbwTfJwRjSP.jpg)
And Beyoncé’s “Lemonade” (#32).
![Image 7: Lemonade](https://pudding.cool/2024/03/greatest-music/assets/album_art_resized/256/7dK54iZuOxXFarGhXwEXfF.jpg)
And Frank Ocean’s “Blonde” (#79).
![Image 8: Blonde](https://pudding.cool/2024/03/greatest-music/assets/album_art_resized/256/3mH6qwIy9crq0I9YQbOuDf.jpg)
But other additions had been out for a long time, like Kate Bush’s “Hounds of Love,” originally released in 1985.
![Image 9: Hounds of Love](https://pudding.cool/2024/03/greatest-music/assets/album_art_resized/256/5G5UwqPsxDKpxJLX4xsyuh.jpg)
And Joy Division’s “Unknown Pleasures” (1979).
![Image 10: Unknown Pleasures](https://pudding.cool/2024/03/greatest-music/assets/album_art_resized/256/5Dgqy4bBg09Rdw7CQM545s.jpg)
Some new additions came from even further in the past. Billie Holiday’s “Lady in Satin” made the list in 2020 despite being unranked in 2003, 45 years after its release.
![Image 11: Lady in Satin](https://pudding.cool/2024/03/greatest-music/assets/album_art_resized/256/4LrLP7DM1KBj8r2Sc098JA.jpg)
In short, beyond accounting for new releases, there must be other factors influencing _Rolling Stone_’s choices.
This project uses _Rolling Stone_ album rankings – twenty years apart in time – to determine what influences “greatness”.
First, musical greatness is shaped by how we listen.
Medium
Just a moment ago, we noted the turnover in _Rolling Stone_’s 2020 ranking: a third of the albums from 2003 did not make the 2020 list.
The Remaining Top 10
#251 - 500
#1 Greatest Album
Rolling Stone’s 2003 Ranking of Greatest Albums
![Image 12: Ranked #1 in 2003, Cover art for The Beatles's Sgt. Pepper's Lonely Hearts Club Band](https://pudding.cool/2024/03/greatest-music/assets/album_art_resized/full/6QaVfG1pHYl1z15ZxkvVDW.jpg)
#11 - #249
Here are the 174 albums from the 2003 ranking that failed to rank twenty years later.
We noticed a few qualities uniting these albums that fell out of favor with judges.
18% are compilations or greatest hits albums. These types of albums were popular in the days of physical releases, like CDs, cassettes, and vinyl. Today, official greatest hits collections have largely been [replaced by ever-evolving playlists](https://web.archive.org/web/20230323121538/https://pitchfork.com/features/article/9887-why-the-death-of-greatest-hits-albums-and-reissues-is-worth-mourning/). In short, these types of albums have lost some of their prestige.
6% of the albums are also not currently available on Spotify.
For example, Captain Beefheart’s “Trout Mask Replica” was #58 in 2003. 17 years later, it failed to rank.
![Image 13: Trout Mask Replica](https://pudding.cool/2024/03/greatest-music/assets/album_art_resized/256/NOS124.jpg)
It’s hard for an album to remain relevant if most people don’t have a means to listen to it.
Here we add in albums unavailable on Spotify that still made _Rolling Stone_’s 2020 list. About half of these albums (in red) saw their ranking decline.
Funkadelic’s genre-bending 1978 album “One Nation Under a Groove”, for example, fell from #176 to #360. The album was removed from Spotify during a dispute between Funkadelic frontman George Clinton and his former label, Warner Records.
![Image 14: One Nation Under a Groove](https://pudding.cool/2024/03/greatest-music/assets/album_art_resized/256/NOS116.jpg)
Next up: musical greatness is shaped by what’s widely listened to.
Popularity
Most of the albums ranked were hits when they were initially released. This might not come as a shock, but it cuts against our intuition that pop music is for the masses and truly great music is only championed by critics over time. The data shows the opposite.
**Billboard #1 Album:** 30% of albums
Top 100 Albums in the 2020 Ranking
**Billboard #2-100:** 60%
**#101+:** 4%
**Never charted:** 6%
**Billboard #1 Album:** 21%
Bottom 400 Albums in the 2020 Ranking
**Billboard #2-100:** 51%
**#101+:** 9%
**Never charted:** 18%
Here we depict the 2020 ranking, but the importance of popularity was clear across all three of _Rolling Stone_’s lists.
When we just look at albums ranked in _Rolling Stone_’s top 100, 30% charted at #1 on the _Billboard_ charts. Furthermore, 96% of albums were _Billboard_ hits at some point.
If we look at _Rolling Stone_’s lower ranked albums, meaning those among the bottom 400, they are 3x more likely to have never charted on _Billboard_. In other words, if you want your album to be considered great, it helps if it is also popular when it’s released.
Musical greatness is also shaped by who is voting.
Judges
To construct these lists, _Rolling Stone_ polled artists, songwriters, producers, A&Rs, executives, journalists, and their staff writers. Here is who voted in 2003:
Scanning these faces, something probably jumps out at you …
The large, large majority of the 2003 voters were men. And while it’s difficult to pinpoint the exact racial identity of each voter, we’re confident that white men were overrepresented.
For the 2020 ranking, _Rolling Stone_ – perhaps in an effort to poll beyond the musical tastes of white men – expanded the voting group from 269 to 336 and doubled the representation of women voters. Here are the judges in 2020:
With two cohorts of voters, from 2003 and 2020, we can reflect on how different voter demographics influence which albums are considered great.
2003 Voters
She/her, They/them, 10%
He/Him, 90%
Gender
In 2003, 90% of voters were men. Not surprisingly, voters selected predominantly male performers—nearly 82% of the 500 albums selected were by men.
_Rolling Stone_ published a few ballots of voters in 2003. Metallica’s James Hetfield only had men in his top 10 included. Green Day’s Billie Joe Armstrong was the same. The most gender diverse ballot, among those published, was Britney Spears’s, with Janet Jackson, Madonna, Whitney Houston, and TLC among her top 10 albums.
Wayne Coyne’s Ballot#1 Debut, Bjork, #2 White Album, Beatles, #3 Soundtrack, The Wizard of Oz, #4 Donovan's Greatest Hits, Donovan, #5 Bitches Brew, Miles Davis, #6 In the Court of the Crimson King, King Crimson, #7 Elephant, White Stripes, #8 Dark Side of the Moon, Pink Floyd, #9 Sea Change, Beck, #10 Physical Graffiti, Led Zeppelin
Billie Joe Armstrong’s Ballot#1 Revolver, Beatles, #2 Rise and Fall of Ziggy Stardust, David Bowie, #3 Beggars Banquet, The Rolling Stones, #4 London Calling, The Clash, #5 The Doors, The Doors, #6 Bringing it all Back Home, Bob Dylan, #7 Never Mind the Bollocks, The Sex Pistols, #8 Nevermind, Nirvana, #9 Rocket to Russia, Ramones, #10 Tim, The Replacements
Moby’s Ballot#1 What's Going On, Marvin Gaye, #2 London Calling, The Clash, #3 Closer, Joy Division, #4 Roxy Music, Roxy Music, #5 Marquee Moon, Television, #6 Bryter Layer, Nick Drake, #7 Low, David Bowie, #8 Freedom of Choice, Devo, #9 The Man-Machine, Kraftwerk, #10 Heaven Up Here, Echo and the Bunnymen
James Hetfield’s Ballot#1 Led Zeppelin, Led Zeppelin, #2 Black Sabbath, Black Sabbath, #3 Welcome to my Nighmare, Alice Cooper, #4 Pet Sounds, Beach Boys, #5 Rocks, Aerosmith, #6 Ace of Spades, Motorhead, #7 Van Halen, Van Halen, #8 (pronounced Leh-Nerd Skin-Nerd), Lynyrd Skynyrd, #9 Strangers in the Night, UFO, #10 White Light, White Heat, White Trash, Social Distortion
Flea’s Ballot#1 London Calling, The Clash, #2 A Love Supreme, John Coltrane, #3 Catch a Fire, Bob Marley, #4 Trout Mask Replica, Captain Beefheart, #5 Are you Experienced, Jimi Hendrix, #6 One Nation under a groove, Funkadelic, #7 Blue, Joni Mitchell, #8 After the Gold Rush, Neil Young, #9 Songs in the Key of Life, Stevie Wonder, #10 Horses, Patti Smith
Britney Spears’s Ballot#1 Thriller, Michael Jackson, #2 Rhythm Nation 1814, Janey Jackson, #3 Bad, Michael Jackson, #4 Like a Prayer, Madonna, #5 Off the Wall, Michael Jackson, #6 Whitney Houston, Whitney Houston, #7 The Dock of the Bay, Otis Redding, #8 Purple Rain, Prince, #9 Sign o the Times, Prince, #10 CrazySexyCool, TLC
In 2020, with more women voters, we see a curious correlation with greater gender diversity in the albums selected: albums by women or mixed-gender groups jumped from 16% to 28%.
Next, let’s consider how voters’ ages shape album selection.
Age
Here are the judges, by age group, at the time of voting.
Voters in 2003 and 2020 were spread out among similar age ranges. How might this have affected the albums they selected?
Generation
We had a hunch that albums released during voters’ teenage years would have an outsized impact on their choices, the most formative years for music taste.
Here are judges arranged by the approximate decade of their teenage years.
In 2020, over half of the judges were teenagers in the 1990s, 2000s, and 2010s. This is a stark change from the 2003 ranking, when judges were predominantly of the Baby Boomer or Gen X generation.
Let’s compare judges’ ages with the release years of the 500 greatest albums of all time.
In 2003, for example, only 11 voters (4%) were teens in the 1990s. In the 2003 album ranking, 74 of the 500 greatest albums of all-time (15%) were from the 1990s.
In 2020, the number of voters who grew up in the 1990s jumped from 11 (4%) to 90 (25%). Albums ranked in 2020 and released in the 1990s similarly increased from 15 to 21%.
Of course, assessing the past is a messy, imperfect business. When _Rolling Stone_ ranks the greatest albums of all time in 2030, a new cohort of Gen Zers will no doubt elevate albums from the 2000s and 2010s.
Yet, there is still some level of consistency over the decades, especially as we get further from the past.
Here are the 2020 albums by release decade. We’ve highlighted the albums that were _also_ on the 2003 list, 17 years earlier.
’90s Albums
Of the 104 albums from the 1990s on the 2020 list, 55 (53%) were on the list in 2003.
’80s Albums
Of the 73 albums from the 1980s on the 2020 list, 56 (76%) were on the list in 2003.
’70s Albums
Of the 155 albums from the 1970s on the 2020 list, 128 (83%) were on the list in 2003.
’60s Albums
Of the 71 albums from the 1960s on 2020 list, 65 (92%) were on the list in 2003.
’50s Albums
Of the 10 albums from the 1950s on the 2020 list, 8 (80%) were on the in 2003.
In short, after a certain point, when people are talking about great albums of the 1950s, they are likely talking about Miles Davis’s “Kind of Blue,” Elvis Presley’s self-titled album, and Frank Sinatra’s “In the Wee Small Hours,” among a few others.
Is it possible in 100 years that some obscure album from the 1950s will suddenly be hailed as the decade’s masterpiece? Yes. But it’s not likely. Some level of consensus does seem to appear over time, despite all of the unexpected non-musical factors that influence list construction.
### Methods
This project began with a Google sheet created by [Chris Eckert](https://twitter.com/kennybloggins/status/1308568487888064518?s=46), [Rolling Stone's 500 Greatest Albums 2003 v 2012 v. 2020](https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1QguM-JM3LAJuZlnmY8aN0MutBJrZAzDs3aWZWTtF1WU/edit#gid=0).
This dataset is actually misleading, because the 2003 ranking seems to come from a book published by _Rolling Stone_, where the editor chose to change the original ranking: "For the book version of the RS 500 I have eliminated a few compilation albums that simply repeated material appearing elsewhere on albums that made the list. I've also combined the two volumes of Robert Johnson's ‘King of the Delta Blues Singers’ into the more readily available ‘Complete Recordings.’ That left room for eight new albums to bubble up from the bottom of our tally."
For this project, we decided to use _Rolling Stone’s_ original ranking, which you can find on the Internet Archive [here](https://web.archive.org/web/20090307145059/http://www.rollingstone.com/news/story/5938174/the_rs_500_greatest_albums_of_all_time/5). (We also acquired the original print magazine issue, published in 2003). The 2003 judges come from the magazine and book. 2020 judges are available [here](https://www.rollingstone.com/music/music-news/voters-500-greatest-albums-list-1062225/)).
You can access our full dataset [here](https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1c_Tdnm7S1oo8R9UNtdCVIY7bYASmf_cvMynOJTpKuHA/edit#gid=0).

print("\nF8")
print(a[a['2020 Rank'].notna()].assign(never=lambda d: d['Peak Billboard Position'].eq(201), group=lambda d: np.where(d['2020 Rank'].le(100), 'top100', 'bottom400')).groupby('group')['never'].agg(['sum','count','mean']).assign(ratio=lambda d: d.loc['bottom400','mean']/d.loc['top100','mean']))
print("\nF9")
print(v.loc[v['Year'].eq(2003), 'Gender'].eq('man').agg(['sum','count','mean']))
print("\nF10")
print(a.loc[a['2003 Rank'].notna(), 'Artist Gender'].eq('Male').agg(['sum','count','mean']))
print("\nF11")
print(v.assign(woman=v['Gender'].eq('woman')).groupby('Year')['woman'].agg(['sum','count','mean']))
print("\nF12")
print(v.loc[v['Year'].eq(2020), 'Teenage Decade'].isin(['1990s','2000s','2010s']).agg(['sum','count','mean']))
print("\nF13")
print(v.loc[v['Year'].eq(2003), 'Teenage Decade'].eq('1990s').agg(['sum','count','mean']))
print("\nF14")
print(a[a['2020 Rank'].notna()].assign(decade=lambda d: d['Release Year']//10*10).query('1950 <= decade <= 1990').groupby('decade').agg(n=('Album','size'), on_2003=('2003 Rank', lambda s: s.notna().sum())).assign(share=lambda d: d['on_2003']/d['n']*100))
EOF
